options.a: Temporary preservation, sanitation, and restoration
options.b: Permanent preservation, sterilization, and identification
options.c: Legal compliance, since every state requires it

distractorExplanations.b: Embalming preservation is temporary, and it disinfects rather than sterilizes; identification is a separate procedure.
distractorExplanations.c: No state requires embalming in every case; the FTC Funeral Rule bars claiming it is legally required when it is not.
distractorExplanations.d: Determining cause of death and sampling tissue are autopsy and pathology functions, not purposes of embalming.

funeral-service-arts-readiness-check-mor.explanation: Temporary preservation, sanitation, and restoration presentation goals. These serve presentation goals for viewing.

options.a: Vascular system distribution of preservative chemicals
options.b: Direct trocar injection of cavity fluid into the organs
options.c: Hypodermic injection of fluid into localized tissue
options.d: Surface packs of preservative gel on the skin

distractorExplanations.b: Trocar injection of cavity fluid into the viscera is cavity treatment, which follows arterial injection.
distractorExplanations.c: Hypodermic injection is a supplemental method for areas arterial fluid did not reach, not arterial injection itself.
distractorExplanations.d: Surface compresses and gels are supplemental surface embalming, not distribution through the vascular system.

options.a: Vessel drainage before injection
options.b: Feature setting before injection
options.c: Hollow organs after aspiration

distractorExplanations.a: Venous drainage belongs to the arterial phase; cavity treatment targets the hollow viscera after aspiration.
distractorExplanations.b: Setting the features (eyes, mouth) is a pre-embalming step, not a function of cavity treatment.
distractorExplanations.d: Topical gels are surface embalming; cavity treatment injects cavity fluid into the trunk organs.

options.a: Postmortem cooling of the body
options.b: Postmortem settling of the blood
options.c: Postmortem stiffening of muscles

distractorExplanations.a: Postmortem cooling of the body is algor mortis, not rigor mortis.
distractorExplanations.b: Gravitational settling of blood into dependent areas is livor mortis, not rigor mortis.
distractorExplanations.d: Muscle relaxation is primary flaccidity (before rigor) or secondary flaccidity (after rigor passes), not rigor itself.

options.a: Settling of blood in dependent parts
options.b: Stiffening of muscles after death
options.c: Cooling of the body after death
options.d: Clotting of blood in the vessels

distractorExplanations.b: Postmortem muscle stiffening is rigor mortis, a different postmortem change from livor mortis.
distractorExplanations.c: Postmortem cooling toward ambient temperature is algor mortis, not lividity.
distractorExplanations.d: Intravascular clotting is postmortem coagulation; livor is the gravitational settling of blood that causes discoloration.

options.a: Postmortem stiffening
options.b: Postmortem discoloration
options.c: Postmortem cooling

distractorExplanations.a: Postmortem stiffening of the muscles is rigor mortis, not algor mortis.
distractorExplanations.b: Postmortem discoloration from settled blood describes livor mortis; algor refers to cooling.
distractorExplanations.d: Postmortem drying of tissue is desiccation (dehydration), a separate change from algor mortis.

options.a: Cavity aspiration and trocar button work
options.b: Cosmetizing only, without wax or filler
options.c: Feature building and wax work for viewing

distractorExplanations.a: Aspiration and trocar buttons are part of cavity embalming, not restorative art.
distractorExplanations.b: Restorative art goes beyond cosmetics to include wax, filler, and feature reconstruction for viewing.
distractorExplanations.d: Clothing and casket interiors are arrangement and merchandise choices, not restorative art techniques.

options.a: Cavity treatment workflows
options.b: Arterial injection of the vessels
options.c: Hypodermic tissue treatment

distractorExplanations.b: Arterial injection uses the injection machine; the aspirator and trocar are cavity-treatment equipment.
distractorExplanations.c: Hypodermic treatment uses a syringe or needle injector for local areas; aspiration equipment serves cavity treatment.
distractorExplanations.d: Feature setting uses eye caps and mouth closure devices, not aspiration equipment.

options.a: Casket choice and service date ahead of body condition
options.b: Condition, cause/manner context, and restoration needs
options.c: A single standard fluid strength for every case
options.d: Cause of death alone, ignoring body condition

distractorExplanations.a: Case analysis evaluates the body's condition first; merchandise and scheduling do not drive fluid and technique choices.
distractorExplanations.c: Case analysis exists to tailor fluid strength and volume to each body, not to apply one standard solution.
distractorExplanations.d: Cause of death is one factor; case analysis also weighs body condition, edema, discoloration, and restoration needs.

options.a: Heavier cosmetics to mask swelling and odor
options.b: Standard arterial fluid and routine handling
options.c: Recognition and appropriate treatment strategies
options.d: Faster viewing in place of treatment

distractorExplanations.a: Cosmetics do not stop gas gangrene; tissue gas needs recognition, special chemicals, and containment.
distractorExplanations.b: Tissue gas (Clostridium perfringens) spreads and needs specialized chemicals and precautions, not routine treatment.
distractorExplanations.d: Rushing to viewing does not halt tissue gas, which can spread quickly; treatment is required.

options.a: Higher-index formaldehyde fluid to bleach it
options.b: Special fluid/cosmetic considerations
options.c: Routine fluids, since jaundice fades after death

distractorExplanations.a: Strong formaldehyde oxidizes bilirubin to biliverdin and turns jaundiced skin green; jaundice fluids are used instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Jaundice does not fade after death and can worsen with routine fluids; it needs special fluids and cosmetics.
distractorExplanations.d: No law requires a sealed casket for jaundice; the case is managed with fluid choice and cosmetics.

options.a: Single-point injection from the right carotid
options.b: Cremation, since autopsied bodies cannot be embalmed
options.c: Additional restoration and vessel considerations

distractorExplanations.a: Autopsy severs the vascular system, so autopsied bodies need six-point injection rather than a single injection point.
distractorExplanations.b: Autopsied bodies can be embalmed; they need multi-point injection, viscera treatment, and extra restoration.
distractorExplanations.d: Autopsied viscera are treated separately with cavity chemical or preservative powder, not skipped.

options.a: Required for exposure control
options.b: Needed for visitors, not staff
options.c: Optional for short procedures

distractorExplanations.b: Embalmers face the bloodborne and chemical exposure; OSHA PPE requirements apply to prep room staff.
distractorExplanations.c: Exposure risk exists in any procedure; PPE is required for every prep room task with exposure potential.
distractorExplanations.d: Gloves alone leave the eyes, face, and clothing exposed; embalming PPE includes gowns, face and eye protection.

options.a: Done after embalming
options.b: Critical risk-control step
options.c: Needed for cremation alone

distractorExplanations.a: Identification must be confirmed before any preparation; identifying after embalming risks preparing the wrong body.
distractorExplanations.c: Identification is required before any preparation or disposition, not just cremation, though cremation makes errors irreversible.
distractorExplanations.d: Paperwork can be wrong; physical identification (tags, bracelets) is verified against records before preparation.

options.a: State funeral board rules and FTC Funeral Rule themes
options.b: Federal licensing rules issued by the FTC for every state
options.c: OSHA standards, which replace state board rules
options.d: Cemetery association bylaws in place of state law

distractorExplanations.b: Licensing is a state function; the FTC Funeral Rule governs price disclosure and practices, not licenses.
distractorExplanations.c: OSHA covers workplace safety; it does not replace state funeral board licensing and practice rules.
distractorExplanations.d: Association bylaws do not override state law; funeral directors follow state board rules and the FTC Rule.

funeral-service-arts-readiness-check-law.explanation: State funeral board rules and FTC Funeral Rule themes where applicable. Each applies where applicable.

options.a: Required by federal law for any body held over 24 hours
options.b: Required by the FTC Funeral Rule before any public viewing
options.c: Required before cremation in most states
options.d: Not universally legally required; rules vary by circumstance

distractorExplanations.a: No federal law requires embalming; some states require embalming or refrigeration after a set time.
distractorExplanations.b: The FTC Rule bars telling families embalming is legally required; a viewing requirement may be firm policy, not federal law.
distractorExplanations.c: Embalming is not required for direct cremation; the FTC Rule requires disclosing that families may decline it.

funeral-service-arts-readiness-check-law.explanation: Not universally legally required for every death; rules vary by circumstance. It is not required for every death.

options.a: Assumed once the family chooses a public viewing
options.b: Obtained from any adult relative who calls first
options.c: Obtained after embalming if the family was unreachable
options.d: Obtained per law/policy from proper authorizing party

distractorExplanations.a: Express permission is required; choosing a viewing does not authorize embalming under the FTC Funeral Rule.
distractorExplanations.b: Authorization comes from the legal next of kin or designated agent under state priority, not the first caller.
distractorExplanations.c: Permission is obtained before embalming; the FTC Rule limits charging for embalming done without prior approval.

options.a: Is handled by the FTC under the Funeral Rule
options.b: Is completed by the family's attorney
options.c: Follows state vital records procedures
options.d: Is filed by the cemetery after burial

distractorExplanations.a: The FTC Rule covers pricing and disclosures; death certificates are state vital records, not FTC filings.
distractorExplanations.b: Funeral directors typically file the death certificate with the physician's medical certification; attorneys do not.
distractorExplanations.d: The death certificate is filed before disposition, usually to obtain the burial or cremation permit.

options.a: Can rest on a phone call from any relative
options.b: Uses the same form as embalming consent
options.c: Skips ID checks when a permit is on file

distractorExplanations.a: Cremation needs written authorization from the legal authorizing agent; a call from any relative is not enough.
distractorExplanations.b: Cremation authorization is a separate, specific document with its own permit; embalming consent does not cover it.
distractorExplanations.c: A permit does not replace positive identification; cremation is irreversible, so ID is verified before it.

options.a: Allowed if printed on the price list
options.b: Allowed when made verbally
options.c: Prohibited themes under the Rule

distractorExplanations.a: Printing a false legal claim on the GPL makes it a written misrepresentation; the Rule prohibits it anywhere.
distractorExplanations.b: The Funeral Rule prohibits misrepresentations whether oral or written.
distractorExplanations.d: The Funeral Rule applies to funeral providers; misrepresenting legal requirements is barred for them.

options.a: Marked up without disclosure
options.b: Bundled into the basic services fee
options.c: Left off the itemized statement

distractorExplanations.a: The Rule requires disclosing when the provider charges more than its cost or receives a rebate on cash advance items.
distractorExplanations.b: The basic services fee is a separate non-declinable charge; cash advance items are listed and disclosed separately.
distractorExplanations.c: Cash advance items belong on the itemized statement of goods and services selected, with any markup disclosed.

options.a: GPL pricing disclosures
options.b: Vital records filing
options.c: Prep room safety programs

distractorExplanations.a: Price disclosures fall under the FTC Funeral Rule; OSHA bloodborne pathogen rules govern prep room safety.
distractorExplanations.b: Death certificate filing is a state vital records process, unrelated to OSHA bloodborne pathogen rules.
distractorExplanations.d: Preneed trusts are regulated by state preneed or insurance law, not OSHA bloodborne pathogen standards.

options.a: Facility access and accommodations
options.b: Embalming fluid exposure limits
options.c: Pricing disclosures on the GPL

distractorExplanations.b: Formaldehyde exposure limits come from OSHA's formaldehyde standard, not the Americans with Disabilities Act.
distractorExplanations.c: GPL disclosures are FTC Funeral Rule requirements; the ADA addresses access and accommodation.
distractorExplanations.d: Preneed cancellation rights come from state preneed law, not the ADA.

options.a: By state insurance/funeral preneed frameworks
options.b: By the FTC Funeral Rule, the same in every state
options.c: By federal banking law through the FDIC

distractorExplanations.b: The FTC Rule governs price disclosure; preneed trusting and insurance requirements differ by state.
distractorExplanations.c: FDIC insurance covers bank deposits, not preneed contracts; preneed regulation is a state matter.
distractorExplanations.d: Associations do not regulate preneed sales; state insurance and funeral boards do.

funeral-service-arts-readiness-check-law.explanation: By state insurance/funeral preneed frameworks varying by jurisdiction. These frameworks vary by jurisdiction.

options.a: Whichever relative contacts the funeral home first
options.b: The person who signs and pays for the funeral
options.c: The funeral director's professional judgment
options.d: State priority of rights / authorizing agent rules

distractorExplanations.a: Custody follows the state priority list (e.g., designated agent, spouse, adult children), not who calls first.
distractorExplanations.b: Paying for the funeral does not confer the legal right to control disposition under state priority rules.
distractorExplanations.c: The funeral director follows the state's right-of-disposition statute and does not choose the authorizing party.

options.a: Share medical details with any caller who asks
options.b: Protect family privacy per ethics/law
options.c: Post cause of death in the obituary by default
options.d: Disclose details to the press for publicity

distractorExplanations.a: Releasing medical or death details to callers breaches family privacy and ethics; details go only to authorized parties.
distractorExplanations.c: Cause of death appears in an obituary only if the family chooses; including it by default violates privacy.
distractorExplanations.d: Using death details for publicity breaches confidentiality and professional ethics codes.

options.a: A fixed sequence of five stages that everyone follows
options.b: A disorder that requires clinical treatment
options.c: A process that should resolve within a year
options.d: A normal response to loss with varied expressions

distractorExplanations.a: Kübler-Ross's stages are not a fixed universal sequence; grief varies in order, intensity, and expression.
distractorExplanations.b: Normal grief is not a disorder; only complicated or prolonged grief may need clinical treatment.
distractorExplanations.c: There is no fixed timeline for normal grief; expecting resolution within a year pathologizes ordinary mourning.

options.a: After the funeral when support fades
options.b: Before a death when loss is expected
options.c: Years later when grief resurfaces
options.d: When the loss is not socially recognized

distractorExplanations.a: Grief that intensifies after support fades is ordinary post-loss or delayed grief, not anticipatory grief.
distractorExplanations.c: Grief that surfaces years later describes delayed grief, not anticipatory grief before the death.
distractorExplanations.d: A loss that society does not recognize produces disenfranchised grief, not anticipatory grief.

options.a: Counseling by the funeral director in place of referral
options.b: Encouragement to move on after the funeral
options.c: Waiting a few months before anyone intervenes
options.d: Referral to appropriate mental health resources

distractorExplanations.a: Treating complicated grief is outside a funeral director's scope; the right step is referral to licensed professionals.
distractorExplanations.b: Urging a family to move on dismisses complicated grief, which needs professional support, not pressure.
distractorExplanations.c: Signs of complicated grief warrant timely referral; waiting months can deepen impairment.

options.a: Family income and the cost of the funeral
options.b: Developmental age and explanations given
options.c: Whether they attended the viewing

distractorExplanations.a: Income and funeral cost do not determine a child's grasp of death; cognitive development does.
distractorExplanations.c: Attending a viewing can help, but understanding of death depends on developmental age and how adults explain it.
distractorExplanations.d: Birth order is not what shapes a child's concept of death; developmental stage and honest explanation are.

options.a: Summarizing options quickly so the family can decide
options.b: Attending to content and emotion without rushing to sell
options.c: Taking detailed notes while avoiding eye contact
options.d: Offering advice as soon as the family pauses

distractorExplanations.a: Rushing to options before hearing the family is directing, not active listening.
distractorExplanations.c: Notes are fine, but avoiding eye contact signals disengagement; active listening attends to emotion as well as facts.
distractorExplanations.d: Jumping in with advice at every pause cuts off the family; active listening lets them finish and reflects back.

options.a: Followed even where they conflict with law
options.b: Respected within legal/ethical bounds
options.c: Standardized to the firm's usual service
options.d: Accommodated if the family pays a fee

distractorExplanations.a: Customs are honored within the law; practices that violate health or disposition laws cannot be carried out.
distractorExplanations.c: Standardizing every service ignores the family's faith and culture; practices are accommodated, not replaced.
distractorExplanations.d: Respect for religious practice is an ethical duty, not a paid add-on; legitimate service costs are listed on the GPL.

options.a: Grief that begins before a death
options.b: Losses not socially acknowledged
options.c: Grief that lasts longer than a year
options.d: Grief that is delayed for years

distractorExplanations.a: Grief that starts before an expected death is anticipatory grief, not disenfranchised grief.
distractorExplanations.c: Grief with prolonged, impairing duration describes prolonged grief disorder, not disenfranchised grief.
distractorExplanations.d: Grief that emerges long after the loss is delayed grief; disenfranchised grief is unrecognized by society.

options.a: Replace referrals to licensed counselors
options.b: Diagnose complicated grief
options.c: Collect unpaid balances gently

distractorExplanations.a: Aftercare complements but does not replace referral; clinical grief needs licensed mental health professionals.
distractorExplanations.b: Diagnosing grief disorders is a clinical task outside funeral service scope; aftercare offers support and referral.
distractorExplanations.c: Aftercare is a support service for families, not a collections tool for outstanding accounts.

options.a: Avoiding the word suicide and any mention of it
options.b: Advising a closed casket and private service
options.c: Sensitive communication and nonjudgmental support
options.d: Explaining warning signs the family missed

distractorExplanations.a: Avoidance adds to stigma; plain, respectful language ("died by suicide") supports the family better.
distractorExplanations.b: Service choices belong to the family; suicide does not call for steering them toward a closed or private service.
distractorExplanations.d: Pointing out missed warning signs fuels guilt and blame; support should be nonjudgmental.

options.a: Confronting reality and beginning mourning tasks
options.b: Ensuring complete closure for every member of the family
options.c: Meeting a legal viewing requirement
options.d: Avoiding the need for a funeral service

distractorExplanations.b: Viewing can help some mourners accept the death, but no ritual ensures closure for everyone.
distractorExplanations.c: No law requires a viewing; it is a family choice that can support the mourning process.
distractorExplanations.d: A viewing is part of the service options, not a replacement that removes the need for a funeral.

options.a: Close friendships with families after the service
options.b: Professional roles without exploitation
options.c: Sharing personal grief to build rapport

distractorExplanations.a: Personal friendships with client families blur professional boundaries and invite dependency or exploitation.
distractorExplanations.c: Self-disclosure of the director's own grief shifts focus away from the family and blurs professional roles.
distractorExplanations.d: Accepting estate gifts creates conflicts of interest and potential exploitation of grieving families.

options.a: Side with the relative paying for the funeral
options.b: Follow majority vote of the relatives present
options.c: Delay services until the family agrees on everything
options.d: Stay calm, document, follow legal authorizing party rules

distractorExplanations.a: Payment does not confer legal authority; the director follows the state's right-of-disposition order.
distractorExplanations.b: Disposition decisions follow the legal authorizing party, not a family vote among whoever is present.
distractorExplanations.c: Indefinite delay is not required; the legal authorizing agent decides, with documentation of the conflict.

options.a: Understanding and reflecting their feelings
options.b: Taking on the family’s crisis as your own
options.c: Acknowledging the family's loss aloud

distractorExplanations.a: Understanding and reflecting feelings is what empathy is; the contrast is with over-identifying with the family's crisis.
distractorExplanations.c: Acknowledging the loss is an expression of empathy, not something empathy differs from.
distractorExplanations.d: Nonjudgmental listening is a core empathic skill, so it is part of empathy rather than its contrast.

funeral-service-arts-readiness-check-psy.explanation: Taking on the family’s crisis as your own unprofessionally. Over-identifying this way is unprofessional.

options.a: Diagnostic, naming the disorder you suspect
options.b: Vague, to avoid upsetting the family
options.c: Paired with a paid counseling package

distractorExplanations.a: Naming a suspected disorder is diagnosis, which is outside a funeral director's license and scope.
distractorExplanations.b: Vague referrals leave families unsure where to go; referral language should be clear and compassionate.
distractorExplanations.c: Selling counseling packages turns referral into upselling and creates a conflict of interest.

options.a: Package prices without individual items
options.b: Casket prices only, on a separate list
options.c: Services offered, with prices by request

distractorExplanations.a: The Funeral Rule requires itemized prices for individual goods and services; packages may be offered in addition.
distractorExplanations.b: Casket and outer burial container prices may be on separate lists, but the GPL itself covers goods and services.
distractorExplanations.c: Prices must be printed on the GPL and given to families at the start of the discussion, not on request.

funeral-service-arts-readiness-check-bus.explanation: Goods and services with prices per Funeral Rule themes. Itemization follows Funeral Rule themes.

options.a: Buy a complete package at a bundled discount price
options.b: Select what they need with price transparency
options.c: Avoid needing a written statement

distractorExplanations.a: Itemization lets families choose individual items; packages are optional, not the purpose of itemization.
distractorExplanations.c: The Funeral Rule requires an itemized written statement of goods and services selected.
distractorExplanations.d: The basic services fee is the one non-declinable charge; itemization does not let families skip it.

options.a: Merchandise markups alone, not collections
options.b: Timely receivables, preneed, and at-need margins
options.c: Preneed sales alone, not at-need receivables
options.d: Total calls, not when payments arrive

distractorExplanations.a: Markups produce revenue on paper, but cash flow also depends on collecting receivables on time.
distractorExplanations.c: Preneed funds are often trusted and not immediately available; at-need collections drive current cash flow.
distractorExplanations.d: Call volume drives revenue, but cash flow depends on the timing of payments and receivables.

options.a: Funeral vehicles, the building, and prep room equipment
options.b: Caskets, urns, vaults, and related merchandise
options.c: Cash advance items such as flowers and obituary notices

distractorExplanations.a: Vehicles, buildings, and equipment are fixed assets, not merchandise inventory held for sale.
distractorExplanations.c: Cash advance items are bought on the family's behalf from third parties, not stocked as inventory.
distractorExplanations.d: Receivables are amounts owed to the firm, a current asset separate from merchandise inventory.

options.a: GPL formatting required by the FTC
options.b: State licensing of funeral staff
options.c: Supply reliability and cost of goods

distractorExplanations.a: GPL content and format are set by the FTC Funeral Rule, not by vendor relationships.
distractorExplanations.b: Staff licensing is handled by the state board, independent of the firm's vendor relationships.
distractorExplanations.d: Preneed trust rules come from state law; vendors affect supply and cost of goods.

options.a: Office hours, with first calls left for the morning
options.b: Services and arrangements, not removals
options.c: Peak days, with no overnight on-call
options.d: Arrangements, first calls, services, and prep needs

distractorExplanations.a: Deaths occur around the clock; first calls require 24/7 on-call coverage, not next-morning response.
distractorExplanations.b: Removals (first calls) are a core staffing need; leaving them out leaves families and facilities waiting.
distractorExplanations.c: Without overnight on-call coverage, night first calls go unanswered; scheduling covers 24/7 needs.

options.a: Handled verbally to avoid a paper trail
options.b: Delayed until the family calms down
options.c: Documented, prompt, and policy-driven
options.d: Answered publicly online to defend the firm

distractorExplanations.a: Avoiding records undermines resolution and legal defense; complaints are documented.
distractorExplanations.b: Delay escalates complaints; prompt acknowledgment and response are part of good complaint handling.
distractorExplanations.d: Public defensive replies can breach confidentiality and inflame the dispute; follow a documented policy.

options.a: Deceptive claims about legal requirements
options.b: Mentioning specific prices in print advertisements
options.c: Offering preneed planning seminars

distractorExplanations.b: Price advertising is lawful and encouraged; the Funeral Rule targets deceptive claims, not published prices.
distractorExplanations.c: Preneed seminars are legitimate community marketing when accurate and compliant with state preneed rules.
distractorExplanations.d: Truthful price comparisons are permitted; deception about legal requirements is what marketing must avoid.

options.a: One business under a single funeral license
options.b: Regulated together under the FTC Funeral Rule
options.c: Often distinct businesses with different licenses

distractorExplanations.a: Cemeteries and funeral homes are often separately owned and licensed; one funeral license does not cover both.
distractorExplanations.b: The Funeral Rule covers funeral providers; cemeteries fall under it only if they sell both funeral goods and services.
distractorExplanations.d: Cemeteries handle interment and grounds; embalming is a licensed funeral home function.

options.a: Marketing, pricing, and staff scheduling
options.b: Verbal consent to save paperwork time
options.c: Liability insurance coverage in place of written procedures
options.d: ID checks, authorizations, OSHA, and documentation

distractorExplanations.a: Marketing and scheduling are operations tasks; risk management centers on ID, authorizations, safety, and records.
distractorExplanations.b: Verbal consent leaves no proof of authorization; written authorizations are a core risk control.
distractorExplanations.c: Insurance transfers financial risk but does not prevent errors; written ID and authorization procedures do.

options.a: Cases, forms, accounting, and compliance tasks
options.b: Social media posts, not case records
options.c: Accounting alone, kept apart from cases

distractorExplanations.b: Social posting may be one feature, but case-management systems exist to track cases, forms, and compliance.
distractorExplanations.c: Integrated systems link accounting to cases and compliance tasks rather than keeping them separate.
distractorExplanations.d: Obituary and livestream tools are add-ons; core systems track compliance tasks, forms, and accounting.

options.a: Required by the FTC for all directors
options.b: Optional once you pass the National Board
options.c: Often required for licensure renewal
options.d: A substitute for the National Board Exam

distractorExplanations.a: Continuing education requirements are set by state licensing boards, not the FTC.
distractorExplanations.b: Passing the NBE leads to licensure, but many states still require CE hours to renew the license.
distractorExplanations.d: CE maintains an existing license; it does not replace passing the National Board Exam for initial licensure.

options.a: Recommending the top package first to anchor prices
options.b: Telling families embalming is legally required
options.c: Showing the GPL only if the family asks

distractorExplanations.a: Price anchoring with the costliest package is a pressure tactic, not needs-based recommendation.
distractorExplanations.b: Misstating legal requirements is a Funeral Rule violation and unethical sales practice.
distractorExplanations.c: The GPL must be offered at the start of any face-to-face discussion of arrangements, not only on request.

options.a: Fast removal first, with identification done later
options.b: Embalming before the family is reached
options.c: Skipping PPE because the death was from natural, non-infectious causes

distractorExplanations.a: Identification and tagging happen at the removal; deferring ID creates a risk of misidentified remains.
distractorExplanations.b: Embalming requires prior authorization; it is not done on first call before the family is reached.
distractorExplanations.c: Universal precautions apply to every removal; cause of death does not rule out bloodborne exposure.

options.a: Explain options, listen, and document choices
options.b: Present the most complete package first
options.c: Give the GPL after choices are made

distractorExplanations.b: Leading with the most complete package steers the family; quality conferences explain options and listen.
distractorExplanations.c: The Funeral Rule requires giving the GPL at the start of the discussion, before choices are made.
distractorExplanations.d: Families must understand costs before signing; the itemized statement is reviewed, then signed.
